title: $d$-spacing distributions as a probe of nematoelastic response in iron-based superconductors
authors: Wenting Zhang, Ruixian Liu, Tingjun Zhang, Weiliang Yao, Xüe Fu, Hanqing Xie, Ziye Mo, Ting Guo, Kuo-Feng Tseng, Thomas Keller, Jitae T. Park, Fankang Li, Masaaki Matsuda, Avishek Maity, Long Tian, Pengcheng Dai, Xingye Lu
abstract: Electronic nematicity in iron-based superconductors (FeSCs) couples bilinearly to orthorhombic strain, allowing nematic correlations to appear in the lattice response. Here we use neutron Larmor diffraction to measure the temperature-dependent distribution of relative $d$ spacings in electron-doped Ba(Fe$_{1-x}$Co$_x$)$_2$As$_2$, hole-doped Ba$_{0.83}$K$_{0.17}$Fe$_2$As$_2$, FeSe, and Fe$_{1.07}$Te. In Ba(Fe$_{1-x}$Co$_x$)$_2$As$_2$ crystals without intentionally applied uniaxial stress, the in-plane distribution width, $\varepsilon_{\rm FWHM}$, increases on cooling in the tetragonal phase and can be described phenomenologically by a Curie--Weiss-like form. The fitted scale $T^*$ decreases with Co doping and evolves similarly to the nematic phase diagram inferred from elastoresistance, although the two experiments probe different response functions. Related broadening in Ba$_{0.83}$K$_{0.17}$Fe$_2$As$_2$ and FeSe supports extending this interpretation beyond electron-doped BaFe$_2$As$_2$. By contrast, Fe$_{1.07}$Te shows no extended Curie--Weiss-like regime without applied stress, whereas uniaxial pressure produces a strongly anisotropic broadening that can contain contributions from both the field-biased lattice response and inhomogeneous loading. A mean-field model with bilinear nematoelastic coupling and spatially varying symmetry-breaking stress explains the Curie--Weiss-like broadening in terms of the renormalized orthorhombic compliance. Neutron Larmor diffraction therefore provides a bulk-sensitive probe of nematic-related lattice broadening that complements electronic and elastic measurements.
summary: This work uses neutron Larmor diffraction to measure how lattice spacing distributions broaden in iron-based superconductors as temperature changes. The observed Curie–Weiss-like broadening provides a bulk structural signature of nematic correlations, confirming that the coupling between electronic order and lattice strain is a key feature across different doping regimes.
main_problem: To use neutron Larmor diffraction to probe nematoelastic response in iron-based superconductors (FeSCs).
main_result: The temperature-dependent broadening of $d$-spacings exhibits a Curie–Weiss-like behavior, which serves as a bulk structural signature of enhanced nematic correlations.
method: Neutron Larmor diffraction is employed to measure the temperature-dependent distribution width ($\varepsilon	ext{FWHM}$) of relative $d$-spacings in various FeSC materials.
model_or_system: The study focuses on FeSCs like $	ext{Ba}(	ext{Fe}_{1-x}	ext{Co}_x)_2	ext{As}_2$ and $	ext{FeSe}$. The underlying physics involves the bilinear coupling between electronic nematicity ($\phi$) and orthorhombic strain ($\varepsilon_6$), modeled by a mean-field Hamiltonian.
key_observables: In-plane relative $d$-spacing width ($\varepsilon	ext{FWHM}$), temperature dependence of $\varepsilon	ext{FWHM}$, and the characteristic Curie–Weiss scale ($T^*$).
important_parameters: Doping level (e.g., Co doping in $	ext{Ba}(	ext{Fe}_{1-x}	ext{Co}_x)_2	ext{As}_2$), applied uniaxial stress, and temperature relative to the nematic transition.
main_assumptions: The broadening is assumed to arise from coupling between electronic nematicity and lattice strain, which can be described by a mean-field model incorporating spatially varying symmetry-breaking stress.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate crystal structures, reciprocal space configurations, and the temperature evolution of $d$-spacing distributions ($\Delta d$) measured via neutron Larmor diffraction.
paper_structure: The paper systematically measures $\varepsilon	ext{FWHM}$ across multiple FeSC materials under varying doping and stress conditions. It then applies a mean-field model to unify the observed Curie–Weiss-like broadening, showing how this lattice probe complements electronic measurements.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism/superconductivity, the use of structural probes (lattice response) to map out phase boundaries related to electronic order parameters is relevant for understanding symmetry breaking in strongly correlated systems.
